lead: This unit explains where Unix and Linux came from, what makes Linux multi-user and multitasking, how kernel and shell fit together, why open source matters, how distributions differ, and how to begin at the command line. After it you can trace a command from your typing to the kernel and use basic directory and file commands safely.
about: The unit starts with the history that gave Unix its design ideas and Linux its kernel. Chapter 1.2 turns those ideas into the features you meet daily: many users, many processes and loadable modules. Chapter 1.3 separates the privileged kernel from the shell and user programs, so a typed command has a clear path. Chapter 1.4 explains why open source licences matter for cost, control and shared fixes. Chapter 1.5 shows how distributions bundle the kernel with tools and how installation options differ. Chapter 1.6 puts you at the prompt with navigation, listing, viewing, printing and basic file commands. The chapters move from background to structure to practical use, and each later chapter depends on the layer before it.

chapters.idea: Unix began at Bell Labs in 1969 as a small multiuser system; Linux is a free Unix-like kernel started by Linus Torvalds in 1991.
chapters.depth: Timeline of Unix and Linux: Bell Labs work, C rewrite, BSD and System V split, POSIX standard, Minix teaching system, 1991 Linux kernel, GPL. Design principles: small tools, text streams, everything is a file, portable C. Some syllabi call this 'Introduction to Linux and Unix'. Keep dates few and standard; no deep kernel history.

figure.aria: Timeline bars mark Unix work in 1969, the C rewrite in 1973, the Linux kernel in 1991 and Linux 1.0 in 1994.

chapters.example: Arrange these four events in time order and give the gap in years between the first and last: Linux 1.0 (1994), Unix work begins (1969), Linux kernel announced (1991), Unix rewritten in C (1973). Answer: 1969, 1973, 1991, 1994; gap = 1994 − 1969 = 25 years.
chapters.trap: Linux is not a version of Unix source code; it is an independently written Unix-like kernel. BSD and System V are Unix branches, not Linux distributions.
chapters.leave: Kernel internals, process scheduling and file permissions go to Units 4 and 5.

chapters.idea: Linux features let one computer serve many users, run many processes, and add kernel code as modules.
chapters.depth: Define multi-user (separate accounts and permissions), multitasking (time-sharing CPU among processes), modularity (loadable kernel modules, layered design). Explain how login, a shell per user, and a preemptive scheduler support these. Some syllabi list this as 'Design principles of Linux'. Name the three features clearly and do not teach scheduler algorithms.

figure.aria: Three user shells pass requests to one kernel, which loads modules and drives the hardware.

chapters.example: A lab server has 4 logged-in students and 90 processes. Each student gets a shell; the CPU has 2 cores. Explain which feature lets all 4 students work at once and which feature lets the 90 processes share the 2 cores. Name both. Answer: multi-user and multitasking.
chapters.trap: Multi-user is about separate accounts and permissions, not just many terminals. Modularity does not mean the kernel is a microkernel; Linux is monolithic with loadable modules.
chapters.leave: Process states, scheduler policies and user/group administration go to Units 4 and 5.

chapters.idea: The kernel is the privileged core; the shell is an ordinary program in user space that reads commands and asks the kernel to act.
chapters.depth: Draw layers: hardware, kernel (system calls, drivers, scheduler), user space (shell, utilities, apps). Explain user mode versus kernel mode, the system-call boundary, the shell as command interpreter, and utilities as separate programs. Some syllabi call this 'Kernel, shell and user space' or 'OS structure'. Introduce fork/exec only as needed; do not teach system-call implementation.

figure.aria: A stack from user programs through the shell and system-call boundary into the kernel and hardware.

chapters.example: A user types ls in bash. Trace the four steps: shell parses the line; shell starts /bin/ls; ls makes system calls; kernel returns directory bytes and ls prints. Which steps run in user mode and which in kernel mode? Name the two user processes. Answer: bash and ls are user processes; system calls run in kernel mode.
chapters.trap: The shell is not part of the kernel. A command like cd changes the shell's own working directory, so it must be a shell built-in, not a separate program.
chapters.leave: System call implementation, interrupts and scheduling are Unit 5; shell scripting is Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Open source software publishes source code under a licence that lets users study, change and redistribute it, which lowers lock-in and allows shared fixing.
chapters.depth: Define source code, licence, copyleft and permissive licences (GPL, MIT/BSD names). Benefits: auditability, no per-seat licence fee, local customization, community support, long-term use. Costs: support, training, migration. Some syllabi call this 'Open Source software and benefits'. Avoid claiming all open source is free of cost.

figure.aria: Source code goes to community review, then a built package, then users, whose fixes return to the source.

chapters.example: A college needs an OS for 40 lab PCs. A proprietary licence costs ₹8,000 per PC. A Linux distribution has ₹0 licence but ₹60,000 total support. Compute the proprietary licence cost, the open-source total, and the saving against the proprietary licence alone. Answer: 40 × 8,000 = ₹3,20,000; open total = ₹60,000; saving = ₹2,60,000.
chapters.trap: Open source does not mean no cost and does not mean no licence. 'Free' in free software is about freedom, not price.
chapters.leave: Package management commands go to Unit 4; detailed licence text is not needed.

chapters.idea: A distribution packages the Linux kernel with libraries, tools, an installer and a package manager; installation choices set where and how it runs.
chapters.depth: Distro families: Debian/Ubuntu, Fedora/RHEL, Arch, SUSE, with package-manager names only. Components: kernel, init, shell, package manager, desktop. Installation options: bare metal, dual boot, live USB, virtual machine. Mention LTS releases. Some syllabi call this 'Linux distributions and installation options'. Do not teach package commands or partition layout deeply.

figure.aria: A tree groups common Linux distributions into Debian, Fedora, Arch and SUSE families with example package managers.

chapters.example: A lab installs Ubuntu on 30 identical PCs. One clean install takes 25 minutes. Cloning the installed disk to each remaining PC takes 10 minutes. Compare serial install time with install-one-then-clone time; give the saving. Answer: serial = 30 × 25 = 750 min = 12 h 30 min; clone = 25 + 29 × 10 = 315 min = 5 h 15 min; saving = 435 min = 7 h 15 min.
chapters.trap: A distribution is not just the kernel. Ubuntu and Fedora share the Linux kernel but differ in installer, package manager and default tools. Dual boot is not the same as a virtual machine.
chapters.leave: Package install/update commands are Unit 4; file system layout and partitions are Unit 2.

chapters.idea: The command line is a text loop: the shell prints a prompt, reads a command, runs it, and returns; basic commands navigate directories and view or copy files.
chapters.depth: Prompt and command syntax: command [options] [arguments]. Navigation: pwd, cd, mkdir, rmdir. Listing: ls with common options -l and -a. Viewing: cat, more, less. Printing: lpr. File operations at survey level: cp, mv, rm, ln, find (details in Unit 2). Permissions: chmod one-line (details in Unit 2). Vi editor: open, insert mode i, Esc, :wq, :q!. Getting help: man, --help. Some syllabi call this 'command-line interface and basic commands'.

figure.aria: A directory tree under /home/ravi has a notes directory containing b.txt, and a separate work directory.

chapters.example: Start in /home/ravi. Run: mkdir notes; cd notes; pwd; vi a.txt (type one line, save with :wq); cp a.txt b.txt; ls; rm a.txt. Give the final working directory and the files left in notes. Answer: /home/ravi/notes; b.txt remains.
chapters.trap: rm removes files and does not use the trash by default; rmdir removes only empty directories. cd changes the shell's own directory, so a child script cannot change the parent shell's directory.
chapters.leave: Detailed permissions, ownership, file types and deeper cp/mv/rm/find are Unit 2; pipes and scripting are Unit 3.
